quote: Men on flood plains appear to be very much prisoners of their experience
content: The misattribution is real, and the sentence should be credited to Kates. The finding it describes has its own evidence, gathered under controlled conditions. When people learn a risk by experiencing outcomes, rather than by being told the probabilities, they systematically underweight rare events (Hertwig, Barron, Weber & Erev 2004). That is "prisoners of their experience" measured in the laboratory. The citation trail needs repair; the claim does not.

quote: events that have never happened are not recalled, and hence deemed to have probability zero
content: Gallagher's pattern is availability. A community's flood risk does not jump in the year after a flood and then decay over a decade; only its salience does. Gallagher fits the decay with a learning model that includes forgetting (Gallagher 2014), and forgetting a risk that has not changed is exactly the essay's mechanism. On disaster relief, Kunreuther's field surveys of homeowners in flood and earthquake zones found that expected federal aid played little part in the decision not to insure, and that many of the uninsured had simply not thought about the hazard (Kunreuther et al. 1978, Disaster Insurance Protection, book, no DOI). "Probability zero" is the essay's shorthand for "not thought about," and the survey respondents said as much.

quote: damage per flood is afterward so much greater that average yearly damage increases
content: Damage per unit of wealth, normalized nationally, answers a different question from the one the levee effect asks. The comparison that matters is between losses behind a levee and the losses the same place would have suffered without one. There the record matches the essay: protection draws development onto the floodplain, and the rare flood that overtops the levee then destroys more than all the frequent floods it prevented. Burby calls this the "safe development paradox" and gives New Orleans after Katrina as the type case (Burby 2006); the observation goes back to Gilbert White's 1945 finding that flood losses kept rising after federal flood-control spending. Subsidized insurance adds an incentive to build, but that does not remove the cognitive part. The two compound.
